Происходит два изменения сразу: порядок слов становится обычным и время сдвигается, как в косвенной речи.

steps.title: How to change someone's mind
steps.html:
Almost everything we instinctively do in an argument makes the other person less likely to agree. The research on this is unusually consistent, and unusually ignored.

A  Ask people how to win an argument and most will describe the same method: gather the strongest facts, present them clearly, and wait for the other side to see sense. Researchers who study persuasion asked whether this works. In several studies, giving people accurate information that contradicted a firmly held belief produced no change at all, and in some cases the belief grew stronger. The listeners had not failed to understand the evidence. They had understood it and defended themselves against it.

B  One reason is that beliefs are rarely stored on their own. A view about a political question is usually attached to a group of people, a set of experiences and a sense of who you are. Attack the view directly and the person hears something larger being attacked, so they do what anybody does under attack: they hold on harder. This is why an argument between two well-informed people so often ends with both of them more certain than when they started.

C  So what does work? The most striking evidence comes from a technique in which trained volunteers knock on doors and, instead of arguing, ask questions. They ask whether the person has ever known anybody in the situation being discussed. Then they listen, without correcting anything, for ten or fifteen minutes. In controlled trials this approach produced measurable shifts in opinion that were still there weeks later — far more than a leaflet full of facts achieved.

D  Professional negotiators arrived at something similar from a different direction. One of them, who has spent his career teaching this, says that people ask him how to overcome objections and are disappointed by his answer. You do not overcome an objection, he tells them; you make sure the other person believes you have understood it. He advises repeating the objection back in your own words and asking whether you have got it right, and he claims that people will often argue themselves halfway towards you while you are still listening.

E  There is a warning attached to all of this. The techniques that genuinely change minds are the same ones used by people whose intentions are not good, and they work faster on those who are tired, frightened or alone. Nothing in the research says that a mind changed by careful listening has been changed towards the truth. It says only that it has been changed — which is a reason to notice when it is happening to you.

F  What almost nobody wants to hear is how slow the honest version is. A leaflet costs pennies and reaches thousands. A conversation costs twenty minutes and reaches one person. Every organisation that has to persuade people at scale is aware of this arithmetic, and most of them choose the leaflet, knowing what the evidence says. Persuasion, it turns out, is not difficult to understand. It is difficult to afford.

Written for this course. Based on published work on persuasion and attitude change, including studies of the backfire effect and of deep canvassing.

steps.html:
How to change someone's mind

Almost everything we instinctively do in an argument makes the other person less likely to agree. The research on this is unusually consistent, and unusually ignored.

A  Ask people how to win an argument and most will describe the same method: gather the strongest facts, present them clearly, and wait for the other side to see sense. Researchers who study persuasion asked whether this works. In several studies, giving people accurate information that contradicted a firmly held belief produced no change at all, and in some cases the belief grew stronger. The listeners had not failed to understand the evidence. They had understood it and defended themselves against it.

B  One reason is that beliefs are rarely stored on their own. A view about a political question is usually attached to a group of people, a set of experiences and a sense of who you are. Attack the view directly and the person hears something larger being attacked, so they do what anybody does under attack: they hold on harder. This is why an argument between two well-informed people so often ends with both of them more certain than when they started.

C  So what does work? The most striking evidence comes from a technique in which trained volunteers knock on doors and, instead of arguing, ask questions. They ask whether the person has ever known anybody in the situation being discussed. Then they listen, without correcting anything, for ten or fifteen minutes. In controlled trials this approach produced measurable shifts in opinion that were still there weeks later — far more than a leaflet full of facts achieved.

D  Professional negotiators arrived at something similar from a different direction. One of them, who has spent his career teaching this, says that people ask him how to overcome objections and are disappointed by his answer. You do not overcome an objection, he tells them; you make sure the other person believes you have understood it. He advises repeating the objection back in your own words and asking whether you have got it right, and he claims that people will often argue themselves halfway towards you while you are still listening.

E  There is a warning attached to all of this. The techniques that genuinely change minds are the same ones used by people whose intentions are not good, and they work faster on those who are tired, frightened or alone. Nothing in the research says that a mind changed by careful listening has been changed towards the truth. It says only that it has been changed — which is a reason to notice when it is happening to you.

F  What almost nobody wants to hear is how slow the honest version is. A leaflet costs pennies and reaches thousands. A conversation costs twenty minutes and reaches one person. Every organisation that has to persuade people at scale is aware of this arithmetic, and most of them choose the leaflet, knowing what the evidence says. Persuasion, it turns out, is not difficult to understand. It is difficult to afford.
